patient.name: Jamal Osei
patient.complaint: Low mood, poor sleep and no interest in anything for 2 months
background: Made redundant from his warehouse job 4 months ago
Lives alone in a flat in Lewisham
Drinks about 10 units of alcohol a week
No previous psychiatric history; no known drug allergies

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with 2+ weeks of low mood, anhedonia and biological features; the distractors are hypothyroidism, normal grief, bipolar disorder and dementia.

points: Jamal, 26, booked in by his sister.
Feels **low most of the day, nearly every day**, for 2 months.
Stopped playing football and gaming: **nothing feels enjoyable**.
Calling in sick to job interviews; not cooking or showering.

steps.lead: Jamal has **low mood + anhedonia** for far longer than 2 weeks, with clear impairment in self-care and work: this is a depressive episode.

points: Wakes at **4 am** and cannot get back to sleep.
Lost 4 kg; food has no appeal.
Cannot concentrate on a TV programme.

steps.lead: **Early morning waking**, poor appetite, poor concentration and worthlessness are the biological and cognitive features that support the diagnosis.

steps.q: Which feature of Jamal's sleep most suggests a 'biological' depression?
steps.r: **Early morning waking** is the classic biological feature. Difficulty getting off to sleep is more typical of anxiety.

steps.title: Depression vs its look-alikes
head: Feature
Depression
Hypothyroidism
Uncomplicated grief
Pseudodementia
rows: Weight gain, cold, hair loss, heavy periods
Linked to the loss, eases with time

steps.lead: Jamal's job loss is the stressor; we still check **TFTs** and ask about alcohol, because hypothyroidism and substance misuse can mimic or worsen depression.

steps.text: Grief is **not** depression. Time-limited waves of sadness after a loss are normal; pervasive low mood with worthlessness and anhedonia is not.

steps.lead: Jamal hears no voices and has no fixed false beliefs. If he believed he deserved punishment for a sin, think **psychotic depression**: urgent specialist referral.

steps.q: What must every assessment of Jamal's depression include?
steps.r: The key complication is **self-harm or suicide**, so a suicide risk assessment is mandatory in every depression assessment.

steps.lead: Jamal is a young man living alone after a job loss: **suicide risk** must be asked directly, every time.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' where the diagnosis is clinical, PHQ-9 grades severity and TFTs exclude hypothyroidism.

steps.r: **Clinical assessment** is the gold standard. PHQ-9 grades severity; it does not make the diagnosis on its own.

steps.lead: No scan or blood test diagnoses depression: Jamal's history and mental state examination do.

visual.title: PHQ-9 score
visual.label: Jamal 17
visual.caption: 17 is moderately severe; above the NICE threshold of 16 for 'more severe' depression.

steps.text: PHQ-9 scores 9 symptoms from 0 to 3 over the last 2 weeks.

steps.title: Baseline bloods
steps.text: All normal: no anaemia, thyroid disease or diabetes to explain his symptoms.

steps.lead: Jamal's **PHQ-9 of 17** grades severity; his normal FBC, TFTs, B12/folate and glucose rule out the organic mimics.

steps.text: PHQ-9 bands: **5–9 mild, 10–14 moderate, 15–19 moderately severe, 20–27 severe**. NICE treatment choices split at **16**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' where the PHQ-9 and risk decide: low-intensity therapy for mild, SSRI (sertraline) plus CBT for moderate to severe, ECT when life-threatening.

points: Jamal has thought 'everyone would be better off without me'.
**No plan**, no intent, no stockpiled tablets.
Protective: close to his sister and nephew.

steps.lead: Risk comes first. Jamal has passive thoughts only, with protective factors, so he can be managed in primary care. His PHQ-9 is **17**, so not the mild pathway.

steps.title: Choosing treatment
nodes: Assess suicide risk: safe or unsafe?
PHQ-9 <16 (mild) → guided self-help or group CBT
Poor response → adherence, dose, switch, specialist
steps.caption: Risk, then severity, then treatment.

steps.q: Before starting sertraline, what must you ask Jamal about?
o: Previous episodes of mania or hypomania
steps.r: An antidepressant alone can tip undiagnosed **bipolar disorder** into mania.

steps.lead: Jamal has no history of highs, so he starts **sertraline** and is referred for **CBT**: NICE favours combined treatment in more severe depression.

visual.title: Jamal's PHQ-9 on sertraline + CBT
visual.caption: Little change in week 1 (SSRIs take 2–4 weeks); steady improvement after.

steps.lead: Jamal is **under 30**, so review at **1 week**; warn him that anxiety may rise at first. Once well, continue sertraline for **at least 6 months**.

steps.text: Switching **from fluoxetine** needs a **4–7 day gap** because of its long half-life. Citalopram, escitalopram, sertraline and paroxetine can be switched directly.

steps.lead: If Jamal stopped eating and drinking or was at immediate suicide risk, or failed several treatments, **ECT** would give the rapid response needed.
Jamal's plan follows **NICE NG222**, graded with PHQ-9 and diagnosed against ICD/DSM criteria.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: how SSRIs work and why they are slow, why stress and cortisol matter, why early morning waking happens, and how ECT works.

steps.lead: Jamal's mood circuits are thought to have disordered **serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine** signalling, on a background of genes, stress and life events.
Months of stress after redundancy keep Jamal's **HPA axis** switched on.
Jamal's **4 am waking** reflects a disrupted circadian and cortisol rhythm: a melancholic, 'biological' picture.

steps.q: Why did Jamal feel no better after 1 week of sertraline?
o: Serotonin levels have not risen yet
The dose is always too low at first
steps.r: Synaptic serotonin rises within hours; the mood benefit needs **downstream receptor adaptation**, which takes 2–4 weeks.

steps.lead: Sertraline blocks **presynaptic reuptake** of serotonin straight away, but Jamal's mood lifts only after weeks of receptor change.

visual.title: Weeks until SSRIs work
visual.label: Jamal 1 week
visual.caption: Judge response after about 4 weeks at an adequate dose.

steps.lead: Psychotic depression gives **mood-congruent** delusions (guilt, nihilism) after the low mood starts, unlike schizophrenia.
ECT works by a controlled **generalised seizure**, releasing neurotransmitters and driving neuroplastic change quickly.

mcq.q: Which symptom is described as pathognomonic of depression in the notes?
mcq.r: **Early morning waking** is the classic biological feature.

mcq.q: What is the minimum duration of symptoms for a depressive episode?
mcq.r: Symptoms most of the day, nearly every day, for **at least 2 weeks**.

mcq.q: An elderly woman with severe depression appears to have global memory loss. What is this?
Which PHQ-9 range is moderate depression?
Which blood test best excludes a common organic mimic of depression?
Which SSRI is first-line for moderate depression?
How long should antidepressants continue after recovery?
mcq.r: **At least 6 months** after recovery to reduce relapse.
They raise synaptic **serotonin** by blocking reuptake.

mcq.q: Which axis is activated by chronic stress in depression?

prompts.q: Define a depressive episode: core features, duration and the ICD-10 rule.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: two core symptoms plus duration is what makes it depression, not a bad week.

points.why: Present most of the day, nearly every day.
The second core symptom; enough with low mood to start thinking depression.
Shorter dips are not a depressive episode.
Measurable impairment is part of the definition.

points.p: ICD-10: 2 of 3 core (mood, interest, energy) + 2 others
points.why: Reduced energy is the third ICD-10 core symptom.

prompts.q: List the biological and other features of depression.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: early morning waking is the one they want you to name.

points.why: The classic biological feature (notes call it pathognomonic).
Weight gain and hypersomnia also occur in atypical depression.
Can mimic memory problems in older adults.
Observable on mental state examination.

points.p: Worthlessness or excessive guilt; reduced libido
points.why: Guilt can become delusional in psychotic depression.

points.p: Recurrent thoughts of death or suicide
points.why: Always triggers a risk assessment.

prompts.q: What is psychotic depression and how is it handled?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: mood-congruent delusions after the low mood started.

points.p: Severe depression with delusions or hallucinations
points.why: Uncommon, severe presentation.

points.p: Mood-congruent themes: guilt, sin, worthlessness, nihilism
points.why: Content fits the mood, unlike schizophrenia.
Not a primary care watch-and-wait.

prompts.q: What can mimic or coexist with depression, and how do you tell them apart?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: always rule out hypothyroidism and normal grief.

points.p: Hypothyroidism: weight gain, cold, hair loss, heavy periods; check TFTs
points.why: Bradycardia and constipation in the stem point to thyroid.

points.p: Uncomplicated grief: time-limited waves of sadness
points.why: Normal reaction, not pervasive.
Global memory loss and 'don't know' answers, unlike dementia's short-term pattern.

points.p: Coexists with anxiety, chronic illness, substance misuse
points.why: Ask about alcohol in every low mood history.

prompts.q: What is the key complication and what does a suicide risk assessment cover?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: every depression assessment includes risk.

points.p: Self-harm or suicide is the key complication
points.why: Ask directly; asking does not increase risk.
Plans and intent escalate risk.
Stockpiled tablets or weapons raise risk.
Previous attempts are a strong predictor.

prompts.q: How is depression diagnosed and graded? Give the PHQ-9 bands.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: clinical diagnosis; PHQ-9 grades severity.

points.why: No blood test or scan diagnoses depression.
Scores 9 symptoms over 2 weeks.
NICE splits treatment at 16.

prompts.q: Which baseline bloods do you send and why?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: exclude organic causes of low mood and fatigue.

points.why: Anaemia causes fatigue.
Most important organic mimic.
Deficiency and diabetes cause fatigue and low mood.

prompts.q: How do you treat mild versus moderate to severe depression, and what do you check before an SSRI?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: risk first, then PHQ-9 decides therapy versus drug.

points.why: High risk means urgent psychiatric or crisis input.

points.p: Mild (PHQ-9 <16): guided self-help or group CBT, not medication
points.why: Drugs are not first-line in mild depression.
Fluoxetine and citalopram are alternatives.

points.p: Severe: CBT combined with an antidepressant
points.why: NICE recommends combined treatment in severe depression.

points.p: Screen for past mania or hypomania
points.why: Antidepressant alone can precipitate mania.

prompts.q: What follow-up, duration, switching rules and escalation apply to antidepressants?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: age under 30 changes the follow-up interval.

points.p: Review at 1 week if under 30; every 2–4 weeks for 3 months if over 30
points.why: Early activation and suicide risk in young people.

points.p: SSRIs take 2–4 weeks; may worsen anxiety at first
points.why: Warn the patient so they do not stop early.

points.p: Continue at least 6 months after recovery
points.why: Reduces relapse.

points.p: From fluoxetine: 4–7 day gap before a new SSRI
points.why: Long half-life; others can be switched directly.

points.p: Poor response: adherence, dose, switch, specialist; ECT if resistant or life-threatening
points.why: ECT gives a rapid response.

prompts.q: What is the biology of depression, including the role of stress?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: monoamines plus HPA axis.

points.why: Basis for SSRIs and SNRIs.

points.p: Chronic stress activates the HPA axis with sustained cortisol
points.why: Linked to hippocampal changes.

points.p: Early morning waking reflects disrupted circadian/HPA rhythm
points.why: Marks a melancholic picture.
No single cause.

prompts.q: Why are SSRIs slow to work, and how does ECT work?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the delay is receptor adaptation, not serotonin level.

points.why: Synaptic serotonin rises within hours.

points.p: Benefit takes 2–4 weeks: downstream receptor adaptation
points.why: Not explained by the initial serotonin rise.

points.p: ECT induces a generalised seizure: neurotransmitter release and neuroplasticity
points.why: Rapid relief in severe or resistant depression.

glossary.anhedonia: Loss of interest or pleasure in activities that used to be enjoyable.
glossary.early morning waking: Waking two or more hours earlier than usual and being unable to get back to sleep.
glossary.psychomotor retardation: Visible slowing of thought, speech and movement.
glossary.psychomotor agitation: Restless, purposeless movement driven by inner tension.
glossary.PHQ-9: Nine-item questionnaire scoring depressive symptoms over 2 weeks from 0 to 27 to grade severity.
glossary.ICD-11: The WHO's current International Classification of Diseases, used for diagnostic criteria.
glossary.ICD-10: The previous WHO classification; depression needs 2 of 3 core symptoms plus 2 others.
glossary.DSM-5: The American Psychiatric Association's manual of diagnostic criteria for mental disorders.
glossary.psychotic depression: Severe depression with delusions or hallucinations, usually themed around guilt, sin or worthlessness.
glossary.mood-congruent: Psychotic content that matches the mood, such as delusions of guilt in depression.
glossary.nihilism: A delusional belief that oneself, one's organs or the world do not exist or are dying.
glossary.pseudodementia: Severe depression that looks like dementia, with apparent memory loss that improves when mood is treated.
glossary.uncomplicated grief: A normal, time-limited reaction to loss with waves of sadness.
glossary.hypothyroidism: Underactive thyroid causing fatigue, weight gain, low mood, cold intolerance and hair loss.
glossary.TFTs: Thyroid function tests: TSH and free T4.
glossary.suicide risk assessment: Structured questions on thoughts, plans, intent, means, protective factors and previous attempts.
glossary.protective factors: Things that lower suicide risk, such as close family, children or future plans.
glossary.SSRI: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, the first-line antidepressant class.
glossary.sertraline: The first-line SSRI for moderate depression in the notes.
glossary.fluoxetine: An SSRI with a long half-life, so switching away needs a gap.
glossary.citalopram: An SSRI alternative to sertraline; can be switched directly.
glossary.escitalopram: An SSRI closely related to citalopram.
glossary.half-life: Time for a drug's blood level to fall by half.
glossary.CBT: Cognitive behavioural therapy: a talking therapy that changes unhelpful thoughts and behaviours.
glossary.guided self-help: Low-intensity therapy using structured CBT materials with brief practitioner support.
glossary.low-intensity psychological therapy: Brief, structured therapy such as guided self-help or group CBT for milder depression.
glossary.mania: A period of elevated or irritable mood, overactivity and reduced need for sleep.
glossary.hypomania: A milder form of mania without psychosis or severe impairment.
glossary.bipolar disorder: Mood disorder with episodes of depression and mania or hypomania.
glossary.ECT: Electroconvulsive therapy: a controlled seizure under anaesthesia for severe or resistant depression.
glossary.treatment-resistant depression: Depression that has not responded to adequate trials of treatment.
glossary.monoamine: Neurotransmitters such as serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine.
glossary.HPA axis: Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, which controls cortisol release in response to stress.
glossary.cortisol: Steroid stress hormone released by the adrenal glands.
glossary.melancholic: A 'biological' depression with early morning waking, weight loss and marked anhedonia.
glossary.neuroplasticity: The brain's ability to change its connections over time.
glossary.NICE NG222: NICE guideline on depression in adults.
glossary.reuptake: Return of a released neurotransmitter into the nerve ending that released it.

technique.stem: A 34 year old woman has a 6 week history of feeling low most of the day. She no longer enjoys seeing friends, wakes at 4 am every morning and has lost 3 kg. She feels guilty about being a bad mother. She has regular periods and no change in her hair or skin. Her TSH is normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about low mood: check core symptoms, duration and an organic mimic.
Low mood + anhedonia over 2 weeks, early morning waking, weight loss and guilt; thyroid excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Core symptoms plus biological features for over 2 weeks: **depression**.

elim: Adjustment reactions are milder and linked to a stressor; none is given.
Needs a history of mania or hypomania; none is described.
GAD is chronic worry and tension, not anhedonia and guilt.
Normal TSH, regular periods and normal hair make this unlikely.

steps.x: **C. Depressive episode.** Rule: low mood + anhedonia ≥2 weeks + biological features = depressive episode.

technique.stem: A 29 year old man has 3 weeks of low mood, poor sleep and loss of interest in his hobbies. He has no thoughts of self-harm. His GP has taken a full history and excluded physical illness. The GP now wants to grade the severity of his symptoms to guide treatment.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

steps.x: Investigation, but a specific purpose: grading severity.
Diagnosis already clinical; organic causes done; the task is severity.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Severity of depression is graded with the **PHQ-9**.

elim: Imaging has no role in typical depression.
GAD-7 grades anxiety, not depression.
MMSE screens cognition, not mood severity.
Cortisol is not used to grade depression.

steps.x: **D. PHQ-9 questionnaire.** Rule: clinical diagnosis, PHQ-9 for severity, bloods to exclude mimics.

technique.stem: A 41 year old woman has a 2 month history of low mood and anhedonia. Her PHQ-9 score is 8. She has no thoughts of self-harm and no previous psychiatric history. She would prefer not to take tablets.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Initial management: risk first, then PHQ-9 decides.
PHQ-9 8 is mild (<16); low risk; patient preference against drugs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Mild depression: **low-intensity psychological therapy**, such as guided self-help or group CBT.

elim: Reserved for severe, life-threatening or resistant depression.
Medication is not first-line in mild depression.
No high risk or psychosis; primary care manages mild depression.
SSRIs are for moderate depression or above.

steps.x: **C. Guided self-help.** Rule: PHQ-9 <16 and safe = guided self-help or group CBT, not an SSRI.

technique.stem: A 37 year old man started sertraline 10 days ago for moderate depression. He says his mood is no better and he feels more anxious. He asks why the tablets are not working yet. He takes them every day.
technique.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the delayed effect?
o: Dopamine D2 receptors are slowly blocked
Serotonin reuptake is not yet blocked
Sertraline is a prodrug needing hepatic activation
Synaptic serotonin falls before it rises

steps.x: A mechanism question about timing of SSRI effect.
Adherent, early in treatment, initial anxiety: classic SSRI timing.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: SSRIs raise serotonin quickly, but benefit needs **receptor adaptation** over 2–4 weeks.

elim: SSRIs do not act on D2 receptors.
Reuptake is blocked from the first doses.
Sertraline is active; this does not explain weeks of delay.
Serotonin in the synapse rises early, not falls.

steps.x: **B. Downstream receptor adaptation takes weeks.** Rule: SSRI effect at 2–4 weeks is due to receptor adaptation; warn about early anxiety.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man has a 3 month history of low mood. He has stopped going to the gym, which he used to love, and wakes at 3 am most days. He has lost 5 kg and feels a burden to his family. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Core symptoms with biological features over months is depression. Hyperthyroidism would give a tachycardia and heat intolerance.

steps.x: Most likely diagnosis: check core symptoms and biological features.
Low mood, anhedonia, early morning waking, weight loss and worthlessness for months.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Classic **depression**.

elim: No history of mania or hypomania.
GAD is worry and tension, not anhedonia.
Normal pulse and normal TSH and free T4.
No psychotic symptoms.

steps.x: **B. Depression.** Low mood + anhedonia + early morning waking = depression.

practice.stem: A 63 year old woman is brought by her daughter. Over 2 months she has stopped eating and says she is evil and has caused her neighbour's cancer. She hears a voice saying she deserves to die. She has early morning waking and slowed speech. She has no history of psychiatric illness.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Mood-congruent delusions of guilt following depressive onset mean psychotic depression. Schizophrenia gives mood-incongruent psychosis without a depressive onset.

steps.x: Diagnosis with psychotic features: decide whether mood came first.
Delusions of guilt and derogatory voice, congruent with low mood, plus biological features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Severe depression with mood-congruent psychosis: **psychotic depression**.

elim: Delirium is acute and fluctuating with inattention; this is 2 months.
Delusional disorder has no pervasive low mood or biological features.
Lewy body gives visual hallucinations, fluctuation and parkinsonism.
Schizophrenic delusions are mood-incongruent and not preceded by depression.

steps.x: **C. Depression with psychotic features.** Guilt delusions + biological depression = psychotic depression; urgent specialist input.

practice.stem: A 76 year old man has become forgetful over 2 months since his wife moved to a care home. He answers most questions with 'I don't know' and is distressed by his poor memory. He has lost weight and stopped reading. His MMSE is 22/30 with patchy, inconsistent errors. His pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 134/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Pseudodementia is depression mimicking dementia: recent onset, 'don't know' answers and distress. Alzheimer's is gradual with poor insight.

steps.x: Diagnosis in an older man with memory loss: depression or dementia?
Short history, a clear trigger, 'don't know' answers, insight and distress, and low mood features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Severe depression mimicking dementia: **pseudodementia**.

elim: Insidious over years, short-term memory first, with little insight.
Acute, fluctuating, with inattention or a physical cause.
Needs gait disturbance and urinary incontinence.
Stepwise decline with vascular risk factors and focal signs.

steps.x: **C. Depressive pseudodementia.** Rapid onset + 'don't know' + distress about memory = pseudodementia.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman has 5 weeks of low mood and loss of interest in her usual activities. She is tired all the time and cannot concentrate at work. She is asked about her sleep.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding?
practice.e: Early morning waking is the classic biological feature of depression. The other options are features of other sleep disorders.

steps.x: Most likely finding: what sleep change goes with depression?
Core symptoms of depression; asked about sleep.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The classic biological sleep change is **early morning waking**.

elim: A feature of narcolepsy, not depression.
Seen in narcolepsy.
Obstructive sleep apnoea.
Restless legs syndrome, linked to iron deficiency.

steps.x: **B. Early morning waking.** Depression's signature sleep finding is early morning waking.

practice.stem: A 52 year old woman has 2 months of low mood, tiredness and loss of interest. She sleeps badly and feels worthless. She has no weight gain, constipation or cold intolerance. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 128/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Normal FBC, TFTs, electrolytes and glucose exclude the organic mimics, leaving depression. Normal TSH rules out hypothyroidism.

steps.x: Most likely diagnosis: organic mimics have been tested.

clues: low mood, tiredness and loss of interest
no weight gain, constipation or cold intolerance
steps.x: Core symptoms and worthlessness; bloods exclude anaemia, thyroid, adrenal and diabetes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: All mimics excluded: **depressive episode**.

elim: Normal sodium and potassium, no hypotension or pigmentation.
TSH and free T4 are normal.
Haemoglobin is normal.
Glucose is normal.

steps.x: **B. Depressive episode.** Normal baseline bloods + core symptoms = depression.

practice.stem: A 23 year old man has felt low for 6 weeks after failing his exams. He has stopped seeing friends and rarely leaves his room. He says he has thought about taking an overdose and has saved up paracetamol. His PHQ-9 score is 21.
practice.q: Which is the most important immediate risk?
practice.e: Severe depression (PHQ-9 21) with a plan and stockpiled tablets means high suicide risk, the key complication of depression.

steps.x: Complication question: what is the key danger in this depression?
Severe depression with thoughts, a plan and access to means.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The key complication of depression is **suicide**; this man has high risk.

elim: Not mentioned; not the immediate danger.
He is not on treatment.
He has not taken the overdose.
No psychosis described.

steps.x: **E. Suicide.** Plan + means in severe depression = high suicide risk; urgent crisis input.

practice.stem: A 39 year old man has 1 month of low mood, poor sleep and poor concentration. His GP diagnoses depression on clinical assessment and wants to measure severity before choosing treatment. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: PHQ-9 grades the severity of depression. GAD-7 measures anxiety and MMSE measures cognition.

steps.x: Investigation to grade depression severity.
Diagnosis already made clinically; need a severity tool.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **PHQ-9** grades depression severity.

elim: Screens alcohol use, not depression severity.
No neurological signs; imaging not indicated.
Grades anxiety.
Screens cognition.

steps.x: **E. PHQ-9.** PHQ-9 for severity; NICE splits treatment at 16.

practice.stem: A 47 year old woman has 2 months of low mood, tiredness, hair thinning and heavy periods. She has gained 4 kg. Her GP suspects depression but wants to exclude an organic cause first.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: The notes list hypothyroidism (low mood, heavy periods, hair loss) as the key differential, so TFTs come first.

steps.x: Initial investigation in low mood with physical clues.
Hair loss, heavy periods and weight gain are hypothyroid features in the depression work-up.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Check **TFTs** before labelling depression.

elim: No focal neurology.
No Cushingoid or Addisonian features.
Heavy periods here point to thyroid, not a structural cause first.
No bone pain, constipation or polyuria.

steps.x: **E. Thyroid function tests.** Low mood + hair loss + heavy periods = check TFTs.

practice.stem: A 33 year old woman has 6 weeks of low mood and anhedonia. Her PHQ-9 score is 7. She has no suicidal thoughts and wants help but does not want medication. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Mild depression is treated with low-intensity therapy such as group CBT or guided self-help, not medication.

steps.x: Initial management: risk, then PHQ-9.
Mild (<16), safe, prefers therapy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Low-intensity therapy: **group CBT** or guided self-help.

elim: Drugs are not first-line for mild depression.
For severe or resistant depression only.
Augmentation or bipolar treatment, not first-line.
She is low risk.

steps.x: **C. Group CBT.** PHQ-9 <16 = low-intensity psychological therapy.

practice.stem: A 25 year old man with moderate depression starts sertraline today. He has no history of mania. He has no suicidal plans. He asks when he should come back to see the GP.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate follow-up?
o: Review only if he feels worse
practice.e: Under-30s starting an antidepressant are reviewed at 1 week because of early suicide and activation risk; over-30s every 2–4 weeks.

steps.x: Follow-up question: age decides the interval.
Under 30 starting an SSRI: early activation and suicide risk.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Review at 1 week**.

elim: Too late for a young patient starting an SSRI.
Interval for over-30s is 2–4 weeks; he is 25.
Far too late.
Active follow-up is required.

steps.x: **A. Review in 1 week.** Under 30 on a new antidepressant = review at 1 week.

practice.stem: A 71 year old woman with severe depression has stopped eating and drinking for 4 days. She believes she is already dead. She has not responded to two antidepressants. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm, BP 98/60 mmHg and her mucous membranes are dry.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Add lithium and review in 2 weeks
practice.e: ECT is indicated when depression is life-threatening (not eating or drinking) or treatment-resistant, because it works rapidly.

steps.x: Management of severe, life-threatening depression.
Life-threatening (dehydrated), nihilistic delusions, treatment-resistant.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Rapid response needed: **ECT**.

elim: Too slow for a life-threatening state.
For mild depression only.
Too slow; she needs a rapid response.
Too slow and she has already failed two drugs.

practice.stem: A 44 year old man has 4 months of low mood after a long period of work stress. He wakes at 4 am and has lost weight. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 130/84 mmHg. Investigations are shown.
